L173: Theorem 4 (Theorem 22, informal). Let n, m, q1, q2 and B be integers such that q1 > 2Bmq2, DB
L174: be a B-bounded and balanced distribution. If there is a randomized poly(n)-time algorithm Learn
L175: that solves search-LAMn,m,q1,q2 with probability ϵ, then there is a poly(n)-time algorithm Learn′ that
L176: solves search-LWEn,m,q1,DB with probability Ω(ϵ2).
L177: We also provide reductions from search to decisional LAM, from LAM to LWE, and others,
L178: which shows that LWE and LAM are as hard as each other under certain parameter regimes. Please
L179: find more details in Section 3.
L180: It should be noted that most of our reductions, including Theorem 22 as shown above, require
L181: q1 to be at least a polynomial in n. To understand the hardness of LAM over constant modulus q1,
L182: we need to investigate the Arora-Ge algorithm and other algorithms, as detailed in our next two
L183: contributions.
L184: Arora-Ge over Composite Moduli.
L185: Recall that the Arora-Ge algorithm [AG11] is efficient for
L186: solving LWE with prime modulus and small support.

L195: algorithm solves LWEn,m,q,Dnoise in time poly(m) with overwhelming probability.
L196: Let us make three remarks on Lemma 5. First, it applies as long as D < q, meaning that the
L197: size of possible errors can be as large as q −1. Second, in [AG11] the sample complexity was written
L198: as m = CNδq log q. However, a careful examination of their proof reveals that in their application
L199: of the Schwartz-Zippel lemma to the proof, they simplified the lower bound ≥1 −D/q to ≥1/q.
L200: By retaining the original bound ≥1 −D/q instead of performing this relaxation, one can directly
L201: recover the tighter sample complexity stated in Lemma 5. Third, since the Schwartz-Zippel lemma
L202: only applies to prime fields, their analysis does not apply to composite moduli. To the best of our
L203: knowledge, the behavior of the Arora-Ge algorithm over LWE with composite moduli has never
L204: been published before.
L205: We start by analyzing the Arora-Ge algorithm over prime power rings. Our result is as follows.

L217: To prove Lemma 6, we have identified favorable linear algebraic properties of the Arora-Ge
L218: polynomials, which enable us to avoid Schwartz-Zippel and use a more direct analytic approach. A
L219: proof sketch is given in Subsection 1.2. This approach not only extends the Arora-Ge algorithm to
L220: prime-power rings, but also reduces the sample complexity by a multiplicative factor of q/(q −d)
L221: when q is prime. The factor of q/(q −d) can be large when q is much larger than q −d.
L222: By Lemma 6, when gcd(d!, q) = 1 (including the case when q is prime), the algorithm fully
L223: recovers s, which is consistent with the result in [AG11]; when gcd(d!, q) = q, the algorithm gains
L224: no information about s, since the polynomials built in the Arora-Ge algorithm will always be 0;
L225: when 1 < gcd(d!, q) < q, the algorithm obtains partial information about s. Actually, we can do
